title: Passover: it would have been enough
hook: a song counting gifts one by one
tomorrow: Passover: as if you left (Mishnah Pesachim 10:5)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the four children, and the one who doesn't know how to ask. Your line was answer each child. Did you answer someone where they were? Today, a song the whole table shouts. Day six hundred eighty.

Partway through the seder, after a long stretch of reading, the energy in the room changes. Someone starts a song with a chorus of three syllables, and suddenly everyone, including the uncle who's been checking his phone and the toddler who's been under the table, is shouting it. Day, day, enu. Day, day, enu. In some Persian and Afghan Jewish families, people grab scallions from the table and playfully swat each other during the chorus, recalling the whips of slavery. It can get rowdy. And underneath the noise, the song is doing something careful: counting.
screen: `THE ENERGY CHANGES.` → `SCALLIONS IN THE AIR.` → `UNDERNEATH: COUNTING.`

segments.voice: Dayenu means it would have been enough for us. The song walks through the story of the Exodus in fifteen steps, each one a gift. If God had brought us out of Egypt, and not brought judgment on the Egyptians: dayenu. If God had split the sea for us, and not led us through it on dry ground: dayenu. If God had fed us manna, and not given us Shabbat. If God had brought us to Mount Sinai, and not given us the Torah. All the way to the land of Israel and the Temple. Fifteen times, the table shouts: that would have been enough. The Haggadah introduces it with a line: how many good steps God has done for us. The full song appears in an early prayer order compiled in Babylonia by a scholar named Amram Gaon. Some of the lines sound strange if you take them literally. Would it really have been enough to stand at Sinai without the Torah? Teachers have answered in different ways. One answer is that the song isn't making a claim about history. It's training the eye. Any one of these steps, it says, deserved a whole thank-you of its own. Don't let the gifts blur into one big lump. And after the fifteen, the Haggadah adds a final paragraph that turns it around: how much more, then, should we be grateful, since God did all of them. It's easy to give thanks in bulk. Dayenu gives thanks one gift at a time.
screen: `FIFTEEN STEPS, FIFTEEN GIFTS.` · `IF ONLY THIS, IT WOULD BE ENOUGH.` · `A NINTH-CENTURY PRAYER BOOK.` · `HOW MUCH MORE, FOR ALL OF THEM.` · then, large: `IT WOULD HAVE BEEN ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: list gifts that would have been enough. Breathe. Think of one good thing in your life right now, maybe a person. Now break it into steps. If they had only shown up once: enough. If they had only stayed: enough. If they had only made you laugh that one time: enough. Go slowly, one gift at a time, saying dayenu after each, out loud or in your head. See how many steps you find before the bell. The bell holds the time.
Dayenu. It would have been enough for us: the seder's song of fifteen gifts, counted one by one. Today's word.
Your line: it would have been enough. Today, write down three small gifts from your day, each with its own dayenu. Day six hundred eighty.

howItsDone: At the seder, after the telling of the plagues, families sing Dayenu together, with everyone joining the chorus; in some Persian and Afghan Jewish homes, people playfully tap each other with scallions during the song.

original.note: Hebrew: enough for us, from dai, enough.

trapdoor: what you thought: a fun, catchy seder song.
what it means: a slow count of fifteen gifts, each worthy of thanks alone, and then of all of them together.
what a scholar hears: the 'ma'alot tovot' of the Haggadah, preserved in full in Seder Rav Amram Gaon, from Babylonia.
